records.answer:
Excellent! Now I have the complete Work section. Let me summarize it in three sentences based on what the Wikipedia page says:

Based on the Ada Lovelace Wikipedia article's Work section, here is a three-sentence summary:

Ada Lovelace translated Luigi Menabrea's French article about Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine into English and augmented it with seven extensive notes (A through G) that were about three times longer than the original translation, with Note G describing a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers that is often called the first published computer program. She recognized that the Analytical Engine could manipulate symbols beyond just numbers, envisioning applications such as composing music, which represented a fundamental insight into general-purpose computation that anticipated modern computing by a century. While there is controversy over whether she was truly the first computer programmer—with some historians arguing Babbage wrote earlier programs—scholars agree that Lovelace uniquely understood the engine's potential to process any entities expressible through logical operations, not merely quantities.

Based on the Ada Lovelace Wikipedia article's Work section, here is a three-sentence summary:

Ada Lovelace translated Luigi Menabrea's French article about Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine into English and augmented it with seven extensive notes (A through G) that were about three times longer than the original translation, published in 1843 under her initials AAL. Her Note G contained what is often called the first published computer program—a detailed algorithm for calculating Bernoulli numbers—and she recognized that the Analytical Engine could be programmed to solve problems of any complexity, extending far beyond mere number crunching to any process based on logical symbols. Lovelace also distinguished between the mechanical details of computing devices and their logical structure, and her notes included what later became known as "Lady Lovelace's Objection" to artificial intelligence, stating that computers could only do what they were programmed to do.

records.answer:
Perfect! Here's the summary of quotes tagged "love" from the first three pages of Quotes to Scrape:

**Total quotes tagged "love": 6**

**Page 1 (1 quote):**
- André Gide: "It is better to be hated for what you are than to be loved for what you are not."

**Page 2 (4 quotes):**
- Marilyn Monroe: "This life is what you make it. No matter what, you're going to mess up sometimes, it's a universal truth. But the good part is you get to decide how you're going to mess it up. Girls will be your friends - they'll act like it anyway. But just remember, some come, some go. The ones that stay with you through everything - they're your true best friends. Don't let go of them. Also remember, sisters make the best friends in the world. As for lovers, well, they'll come and go too. And baby, I hate to say it, most of them - actually pretty much all of them are going to break your heart, but you can't give up because if you give up, you'll never find your soulmate. You'll never find that half who makes you whole and that goes for everything. Just because you fail once, doesn't mean you're gonna fail at everything. Keep trying, hold on, and always, always, always believe in yourself, because if you don't, then who will, sweetie? So keep your head high, keep your chin up, and most importantly, keep smiling, because life's a beautiful thing and there's so much to smile about."

- Bob Marley: "You may not be her first, her last, or her only. She loved before she may love again. But if she loves you now, what else matters? She's not perfect—you aren't either, and the two of you may never be perfect together but if she can make you laugh, cause you to think twice, and admit to being human and making mistakes, hold onto her and give her the most you can. She may not be thinking about you every second of the day, but she will give you a part of her that she knows you can break—her heart. So don't hurt her, don't change her, don't analyze and don't expect more than she can give. Smile when she makes you happy, let her know when she makes you mad, and miss her when she's not there."

- Elie Wiesel: "The opposite of love is not hate, it's indifference. The opposite of art is not ugliness, it's indifference. The opposite of faith is not heresy, it's indifference. And the opposite of life is not death, it's indifference."

- Friedrich Nietzsche: "It is not a lack of love, but a lack of friendship that makes unhappy marriages."

**Page 3 (1 quote):**
- Pablo Neruda: "I love you without knowing how, or when, or from where. I love you simply, without problems or pride: I love you in this way because I do not know any other way of loving but this, in which there is no I or you, so intimate that your hand upon my chest is my hand, so intimate that when I fall asleep your eyes close."

Perfect! I have all 11 books in the Travel category with their prices. Now let me identify the cheapest one:

Looking at the prices:

- Full Moon over Noah's Ark: An Odyssey to Mount Ararat and Beyond: £49.43
- See America: A Celebration of Our National Parks & Treasured Sites: £48.87
- Vagabonding: An Uncommon Guide to the Art of Long-Term World Travel: £36.94
- Under the Tuscan Sun: £37.33
- A Summer In Europe: £44.34
- The Great Railway Bazaar: £30.54
- A Year in Provence (Provence #1): £56.88
- **The Road to Little Dribbling: Adventures of an American in Britain (Notes From a Small Island #2): £23.21**
- Neither Here nor There: Travels in Europe: £38.95
- 1,000 Places to See Before You Die: £26.08

The cheapest book in the Travel category is **"The Road to Little Dribbling: Adventures of an American in Britain (Notes From a Small Island #2)"** and it costs **£23.21**.

# Go back to the release page
goto_url("https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3130/")

# Find and click the Windows embeddable package (64-bit) link
links = js("""
Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('a')).filter(a => 
  a.textContent.includes('Windows embeddable') && 
  a.textContent.includes('64-bit')
)
""")
print(f"Found {len(links)} links")

if links:
    # Get the backendNodeId for the first matching link
    link = links[0]
    print(f"Link text: {link.get('textContent', '')}")
    
    # Use JS to click the link
    js("""
    Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('a')).filter(a => 
      a.textContent.includes('Windows embeddable') && 
      a.textContent.includes('64-bit')
    )[0].click()
    """)
    print("Clicked the download link")
    
    # Wait a bit for download to start
    import time
    time.sleep(3)
PY
